law.free_movement_answer: NO. Free movement ended 31 December 2020 and nothing since has restored it. In August 2026 an EU/EEA/Swiss national has no right to work in the UK unless they (a) hold EU Settlement Scheme settled/pre-settled status (i.e. were already UK-resident pre-2021), (b) are Irish (Common Travel Area), or (c) hold a work visa. EU nationals can still enter visa-free as visitors for up to 6 months, but since 2025 they need an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) first, and visitor status prohibits ALL work - paid or unpaid, employed or self-employed, even for a foreign employer, even "just helping out". Laying blocks on a Birmingham extension is unambiguously "work"; it appears nowhere in the Appendix V permitted activities (which cover meetings, negotiations, and narrow exceptions like manufacturer engineers servicing equipment under warranty). The UK-EU Trade & Cooperation Agreement (TCA) did NOT preserve the EU posted-workers regime - that is an intra-EU concept that stopped applying to the UK at Brexit. The TCA's Mode 4 (mobility) commitments are limited to business visitors, intra-corporate transferees, and contractual service suppliers/independent professionals, all of which are implemented through UK visa routes with sponsorship and qualification requirements (see company_contract_answer) - none of which a labour-only site crew can meet. Practical upshot: the only "EU tradesmen" the client can lawfully use are ones already settled in the UK under EUSS - i.e. the existing Birmingham labour market (a large share of which is already Polish/Romanian) at the £220-280/day rates he is already paying. There is no lawful way to fly a crew in from Krakow or Bucharest for this job.
law.company_contract_answer: Contracting a Polish (or Romanian etc.) COMPANY to "supply and erect" with its own workforce does not change the analysis: immigration law attaches to the individual physically working on UK soil, not to who invoices. Each of that company's operatives needs UK work authorisation; there is no post-Brexit posting/secondment right. The one TCA-derived route that exists on paper is the Global Business Mobility - Service Supplier visa (implementing the TCA's contractual-service-supplier and independent-professional commitments, Art. SERVIN 4.1), and it is designed to fail this use case on every limb: (1) the UK customer must hold a Home Office GBM sponsor licence and the contract must be registered with the Home Office - a private homeowner cannot get one; (2) the contract must be a bona fide contract not exceeding 12 months awarded through open tendering or an equivalent genuine procedure; (3) each worker must have been employed by the overseas firm for at least 12 months, have 3+ years' professional experience in the sector, and hold a university degree or equivalent-level technical qualification - i.e. it is built for architects, engineers and consultants, not bricklayers and hod carriers; (4) stay is capped at 12 months max. The separate GBM "Secondment Worker" route requires a UK contract worth £50m+, and ICT (Senior/Specialist Worker) requires a linked UK entity and a ~£52.5k RQF6 salary - both irrelevant. So: no lawful route exists for a foreign contractor's site labour on a UK private domestic build. Also worth telling the client: a contract performed by illegal labour is tainted by illegality (enforcement problems if the work is defective), site/public-liability insurance would almost certainly be void, and he as the "final consumer" who arranged it would not escape the enforcement exposure described under penalties.
law.sponsorship_answer: The Skilled Worker route technically covers the key wet trades in 2026, but only via a licensed employer - never a homeowner. Position after the 22 July 2025 rule changes (implementing the May 2025 white paper): the skill threshold went back up to RQF6 (degree level), so RQF3-5 trades like bricklayers, roofers/roof tilers/slaters, carpenters/joiners and retrofitters are only sponsorable because they sit on the Immigration Salary List under transitional arrangements / the new Temporary Shortage List (TSL, in force 22 July 2025) - and those construction entries carry a removal date of 31 December 2026, with the MAC's Stage 2 review (reported July 2026) deciding what survives. New RQF3-5 sponsorships since 22 July 2025 carry NO dependants and no fee discounts. Salary: the general Skilled Worker threshold is now £41,700; RQF3-5 ISL/TSL roles have a £25,000 cash floor plus the occupation going rate (advisers quote effective bricklayer thresholds from ~£33,400 up to the full £41,700 depending on which option applies - i.e. roughly £128-160+/day PAYE before on-costs). Employer machinery: sponsor licence £611 (small sponsor) / £1,682 (large), ~8 weeks standard processing (10 working days with £750 priority); £525 per Certificate of Sponsorship; Immigration Skills Charge £480/yr small (£1,320 large) after the 32% rise on 16 December 2025; visa fees and £1,035/yr Immigration Health Surcharge per worker; typical legal costs £2-10k; further fee rises landed April 2026. Can a homeowner sponsor? No. A sponsor must be a genuine organisation lawfully operating in the UK, offering a genuine vacancy in ITS business, running PAYE, with HR compliance systems and reporting duties. A private individual building their own extension has no employing business and no genuine ongoing vacancy; an application would be refused (and inventing a company to do it is sponsor-licence fraud). Honest economics even for a real builder-employer: £41.7k salary + ~15% employer NI + ISC + fees + 2-4 months lead time per worker is MORE expensive than Birmingham's bottom-of-market labour-only price work (£220-280/day self-employed brickies, blockwork at £17.50-20/m2) - which is why the sponsored route is used by big contractors on long programmes, not domestic extensions. "Import a team cheaper" is economically backwards in 2026: the legal import route costs more than the local market.
law.penalties: Civil penalty (s.15 Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006): since 13 February 2024, up to £45,000 per illegal worker for a first breach and £60,000 per worker for repeats - unchanged and fully in force in 2026 (~£130m in penalties issued in 2025 alone). The scheme applies to ANY employer, including private individuals who employ people (households are not exempt - cf. domestic staff). Criminal offence (s.21 IANA 2006 as amended): employing someone knowing OR having reasonable cause to believe they lack the right to work = up to 5 years' imprisonment and an unlimited fine - a homeowner who knowingly flies in a visitor-status crew sits squarely in "reasonable cause to believe". The workers themselves commit the illegal working offence (Immigration Act 2016): arrest, up to 6 months, wages seizable as proceeds of crime, removal and re-entry bans. Who is the "employer" when a gang is supplied by a fixer/gangmaster? The penalty attaches to whoever engages the worker under a contract of service - tribunals look at substance, not labels, so day-rate labourers directed on site by a self-managing homeowner can be HIS employees; if a labour-only subcontractor genuinely employs them, the penalty lands there, but the homeowner's criminal exposure for knowingly using illegal labour remains. Critically, the loophole for "self-employed" labour closes mid-build: s.48 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 (royal assent December 2025) extends the illegal-working regime and right-to-work checking duties to contracts for services, individual sub-contractors and gig/platform workers from 1 OCTOBER 2026 - the party engaging the individual must check status or face the civil penalty. So the classic "they're all self-employed, not my problem" defence dies during this project's programme. HMRC angles: CIS does NOT apply to a private householder - a homeowner is not a CIS "contractor" (the deemed-contractor rules only catch businesses spending £3m+ on construction), so no CIS registration or 20/30% deductions are needed when he pays subbies; but if the labourers are in substance his employees, PAYE/NIC obligations and National Minimum/Living Wage apply (NLW £12.21/hr from April 2025, rising ~£12.7 from April 2026; HMRC enforces arrears plus penalties up to 200% and public naming). Cash wages with no records compound everything: evidence of evasion, no NMW audit trail, and potential money-laundering exposure for handling the proceeds.
law.grey_routes: These are the routes people actually try, and why each fails: (1) THE TOURIST-VISA/ETA CREW - fly in "on holiday", work 6 weeks, fly home, rotate. Illegal for every worker from the first trowel-lift (visitors cannot work); the ETA application itself creates a border data trail, deception at entry triggers 10-year re-entry bans, and the engager faces the £45k-per-head civil penalty plus the 5-year criminal offence. (2) THE "SELF-EMPLOYED EU CONTRACTOR" - workers invoice from a Polish sole trade or Ltd and claim to be visiting businesspeople. Self-employment in the UK is still work; visitor rules prohibit providing services to UK clients regardless of where the invoice goes; the Home Office looks at what the person is physically doing on site, not the paperwork. And from 1 October 2026 the engager must run right-to-work checks on self-employed subbies anyway. (3) THE FOREIGN-COMPANY "POSTING" - dressed up as (2) at company scale; no posted-worker regime exists post-Brexit and the Service Supplier visa is unusable for site labour (see company_contract_answer), so it is simply illegal working with better letterhead - plus void insurance and an unenforceable building contract. (4) CASH-IN-HAND - doesn't launder any of the above, it aggravates it: no RTW checks, no NMW/PAYE records, evasion evidence, POCA exposure. ENFORCEMENT REALITY 2025-26: construction is a named priority sector for Immigration Enforcement. Raids and arrests are at record levels - 17,400+ raids and 12,300+ arrests between July 2024 and end-2025 (up 77%/83%), £130m in civil penalties in 2025; construction-site enforcement visits Jan-Sep 2025 hit 206 with 477 arrests, nearly triple all of 2024 and the highest in a decade (e.g. 30 arrested in one Swindon site raid, Dec 2025). Domestic sites are not invisible: a £171k extension has planning and building-control visibility, scaffolding on a residential street, and the two most common tip-off sources in the sector are neighbours and undercut rival trades. Bottom line for the client: every import route is either unlawful or more expensive than the Birmingham market he's already buying at; the lawful version of his idea is simply hiring settled EU-origin tradespeople who already live here - which is the existing local market and the rates he already has.

alts.uk_based_gangs: VERDICT: The bill IS already at (or below) the settled Eastern European market rate - there is almost nothing left to shave. 2026 Birmingham benchmarks: a lone bricklayer typically £180-300/day UK-wide, with Birmingham-specific guides showing brickie+labourer £340-440/day and a 2+1 gang £500-600/day (tradedayrates.co.uk, gorabricklayers.co.uk - itself a Polish-named Birmingham firm, which tells you the 'Polish gang' IS the local market now). Labour-only brickwork £80-150/m2; the bill's £17.50-20/m2 price-work blockwork and £220-280/day brickie sit at the bottom of those ranges. Birmingham's Polish/Romanian trade workforce arrived pre-2021, holds settled/pre-settled status (full right to work, verified free in 2 minutes via share code at gov.uk/view-right-to-work - do this check anyway for anyone you directly engage), and has been pricing at UK market rates for years; they are not a discount pool, they largely ARE the bottom-of-market rates already in this bill. Where found: word of mouth at trade counters (Travis Perkins/Jewson/EH Smith Hall Green - ask the counter staff who's buying blocks in quantity), Polish shops and Facebook groups ('Polacy w Birmingham', 'Budowlancy UK'), Bark and MyBuilder listings for Birmingham (Bark shows West Midlands builders at £16-42/hr - i.e. the same £130-340/day span). Realistic capture: 0-5% on labour lines, mostly by re-tendering price-work (per-m2/per-1000-brick) rather than day rate, because price-work transfers productivity risk to the gang. A settled Romanian gang quoting £16/m2 blockwork saves ~£300-600 on a whole extension's blockwork - real but trivial.
alts.uk_registered_firms: Three lawful models exist, all UK-registered/insured/RTW-checked: (1) SUPPLY+FIT WINDOW IMPORTERS - Fenbro (Polish stock, sells into UK/Ireland, handles delivery, customs and coordinates UKAS-type professional installation; shipping from ~£900 for a 5-window pallet set) and Debesto operate exactly the model already in this plan: factory in Poland, fitting crew lawfully working in the UK. This is the proven ~40-50% saving on the glazing package and it is already banked in the £171k bill. (2) TIMBER-FRAME/SHELL KITS WITH UK ERECTION CREWS - Baltic/Polish manufacturers (e.g. WIGO Group Latvia/Lithuania; KD Haus-type kit importers) offer supply-only or supply-and-erect; MoneySavingExpert forum experience puts Baltic kit prices at roughly 1/3 of UK equivalents, BUT the caveats are real: tight factory tolerances vs UK foundation flatness, structural sign-off to UK Building Regs, and this extension is already designed in masonry - switching structure now costs redesign fees that eat the saving. Only worth it if the structural design is still open. (3) WHOLE-JOB POLISH BUILDING FIRMS - long-established UK-registered outfits exist (W2 Polish Builders, since 1999; Polish Builders 4u, since 2005; several on Checkatrade/MyBuilder with strong reviews) claiming 'best deals in the market', and genuinely often quote 10-20% under mainstream main contractors. BUT (a) they are London-concentrated, thin on the ground in Birmingham; (b) their saving is versus a MAIN CONTRACTOR'S 15-25% overhead+margin, which this client has ALREADY stripped out by self-managing labour-only trades - so for this build they would typically come in HIGHER, not lower; (c) due diligence is essential: reviews.io documents one operator cycling through multiple company names (Profit Homes Ltd / Polish Builders London / Polish Trusted Builders / Red Brix Investments) with incomplete-work complaints - check Companies House age, insurance certificates and referenced past jobs, exactly as for any builder.
alts.offshorable_items: Per item, does shipping keep the saving? WINDOWS/SLIDER (already in plan): YES - high value, low bulk, ~half UK price landed even after ~£900+ freight; the one clear winner, already captured. STAIRS/BESPOKE JOINERY: YES, marginally - a bespoke oak/softwood staircase from a Polish joinery shop typically lands 30-50% under a UK bespoke quote (£500-1,500 saved on a £2-3k stair); firms like Canterwood Partnership run the Poland-workshop-to-UK model; a stair fits one pallet space so freight doesn't kill it; check Part K compliance (rise/going/handrail) is specified before fabrication. KITCHEN (if in scope): YES - Polish/Lithuanian cabinetry landed 20-40% under UK bespoke; another pallet-friendly, high-value-to-weight item; template carefully, no site remeasure once shipped. BATHROOM PODS: NO for one house - the industry model assumes volume (bulk orders envisage ~100 units, per greenspec/Building magazine); single-order makers exist (Domczar, Taplanes, pods from ~£1,000 basic) but craneage, access to a B14 semi's rear, design integration and Building Control interfaces erase the labour saving on ONE bathroom; not worth it. CUT ROOF TIMBER/TRUSSES: NO - structural softwood is a commodity the UK already imports at scale; a UK truss manufacturer's design+supply price is already the efficient answer; shipping cut timber from the Baltics saves nothing after freight and you lose the truss designer's Building Regs calcs. DRY-LINING/PLASTERBOARD: NO - heavy, cheap, fragile commodity; freight exceeds any factory-gate saving; and dry-lining is mostly LABOUR anyway, which cannot be shipped. General rule: offshore things that are high £/kg and made to drawing (glazing, stairs, cabinetry); never things that are cheap-per-kg or mostly site labour.
alts.arithmetic: Base: £171k build, labour content ~£55-65k (32-38% of total - consistent with published 40-45% labour share once fees/fixed costs in the £171k are excluded). THEORETICAL MAX: if imported labour were literally free and lawful, the ceiling is £55-65k. Both premises fail. Lawfully importing a crew in 2026 requires a licensed sponsor (a business - a homeowner cannot hold a sponsor licence), Skilled Worker salary floors and going-rates far above these price-work equivalents, plus per-worker sponsorship/visa/skills-charge costs of several £k each - by the time a crew is lawfully here, employed, housed and transported, their cost EXCEEDS the £220-280/day already in the bill; and unlawful routes carry civil penalties up to £60k per illegal worker plus criminal exposure, so the 'free labour' scenario has negative expected value, not zero cost. REALISTIC LAWFUL CAPTURE via routes 1-3: (1) re-tender price-work to settled EE gangs: 0-5% of labour = £0-3k; (2) UK-registered Polish firm for the whole job: ~£0 incremental (their edge is vs main-contractor margin the client already stripped); (3) further fabrication offshoring beyond the windows already banked: stairs £0.5-1.5k + kitchen (if in scope) £2-5k, pods/roof/boards £0 = roughly £1-6k. TOTAL REALISTIC: ~£3-8k, i.e. 2-5% of the build - versus the fantasy £55-65k. The honest answer to 'import a team and do it cheaper': the theoretical prize is ~£60k, the lawful capture is under £10k, and the bill is already priced at the level an imported crew was imagined to deliver, because Birmingham's settled Eastern European workforce already set these bottom-of-market rates.

verdict.legal_verdict: No — there is no legal way to fly in a build crew from Poland, Romania, the Baltics or anywhere else for your extension: EU free movement ended in 2020, a visitor (even with the now-mandatory ETA) is banned from doing any work at all, and every work-visa route requires a Home Office-licensed business sponsor, which a private homeowner cannot be — and contracting a foreign COMPANY to "post" its own workers changes nothing, because UK immigration law attaches to each person physically laying blocks on your site, not to who sends the invoice. If you do it anyway you face a civil fine of up to £45,000 PER WORKER (£60,000 for repeat breaches), a criminal offence carrying up to 5 years' imprisonment for employing someone you have reasonable cause to believe lacks the right to work, void site insurance and an unenforceable building contract — and from 1 October 2026, mid-way through your programme, the law (s.48 Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025) extends right-to-work checking and penalties to "self-employed" subcontractors too, killing the classic "they're all self-employed, not my problem" defence, at a moment when construction is a named enforcement priority (206 construction-site raids and 477 arrests in Jan–Sep 2025 alone, the highest in a decade). The only "imported" tradespeople you can lawfully hire are EU-origin workers who already settled here before 2021 under the EU Settlement Scheme — and they ARE the existing Birmingham labour market that is already pricing your job at £220–280/day, so the lawful version of your idea is the market you are already buying from.
verdict.capture_plan: FRACTION ALREADY IN THE BILL: essentially all of it. The theoretical prize is the labour content of the £171k build, roughly £55–65k — but your bottom-of-Birmingham price-work rates (£220–280/day brickie, £17.50–20/m2 blockwork vs published Birmingham norms of £180–300/day and £80–150/m2 brickwork) ARE the settled Polish/Romanian market rate; the "imported crew" price is already what you are paying. The one genuinely large import saving — Polish factory windows/glazing at ~40–50% below UK supply (Fenbro/Debesto model) — is already banked in the £171k. Even for a real licensed employer, the lawful import route now costs MORE than your bill: £41,700 Skilled Worker salary floor (or ~£33.4k+ effective for TSL trades) + ~15% employer NI + £611–1,682 licence + £525/CoS + £480–1,320/yr Immigration Skills Charge + £1,035/yr health surcharge + 2–4 months lead time = well above £220–280/day self-employed. INCREMENTAL LAWFUL CAPTURE: ~£3–8k (2–5% of build), via three actions. (1) Re-tender the remaining wet-trade packages as price-work (per m2 / per 1,000 bricks, never day rate) to settled Eastern European gangs — found at trade counters (Travis Perkins/Jewson/EH Smith Hall Green), Polish community networks ("Polacy w Birmingham", "Budowlancy UK" Facebook groups), MyBuilder/Bark Birmingham listings: worth £0–3k; verify anyone you directly engage with a free 2-minute share-code check at gov.uk/view-right-to-work (good practice now, effectively required of engagers from 1 Oct 2026). (2) Offshore more FABRICATION, not labour — high £/kg, made-to-drawing items only: bespoke staircase from a Polish joinery shop, £500–1,500 saved (specify Part K rise/going/handrail before fabrication); Polish/Lithuanian kitchen cabinetry if in scope, £2–5k saved. Skip bathroom pods (volume economics fail for one bathroom), roof trusses (UK design+supply already efficient and carries the Building Regs calcs) and plasterboard (freight exceeds saving; dry-lining is mostly labour). (3) Do NOT bother with whole-job "Polish builder" firms: their genuine 10–20% edge is versus a main contractor's 15–25% overhead and margin, which you have already stripped out by self-managing labour-only trades — for this build they would typically quote higher, not lower. Bottom line: imagined saving ~£60k; lawful incremental capture under £10k; the bill is already priced at the level an imported crew was fantasised to deliver.
killed: KILLED (superseded by events): 'the MAC's Stage 2 review (reported July 2026) deciding what survives' — the MAC actually PUBLISHED its Stage 2 Temporary Shortage List report on 23 July 2026, recommending only 28 occupations (down from 82 under review, but including some construction and manufacturing trades) get provisional access from January 2027 to June 2028; the government decision is expected autumn 2026 (bateswells.co.uk 23 Jul 2026; jobbatical.com TSL risk map; howespercival.com).

KILLED (overstated finality): the implication that construction-trade sponsorship definitively ends 31 December 2026 — the interim TSL entries do expire 31 Dec 2026, but the MAC has recommended continued (18-month) access for construction trades from January 2027, so the route may survive in narrowed form; irrelevant to a homeowner either way, who can never hold a sponsor licence.

KILLED (stale tense): 'since 2025 they need an ETA first' — updated: ETA became mandatory for EU nationals travelling from 2 April 2025 and has been hard-enforced since 25 February 2026 (no ETA = denied boarding); it costs £16, lasts 2 years, and confers visitor status only, with zero work rights (gov.uk written statement HCWS1361, 25 Feb 2026; Fragomen).

KILLED (stale tense): 'NLW £12.21/hr from April 2025, rising ~£12.7 from April 2026' — the £12.71/hr National Living Wage is now in force (April 2026), so any labourers who are in substance the homeowner's employees must be paid at least £12.71/hr with PAYE.
